overview.text: In signal processing and statistics, noise is variation or interference in recorded data that is not the information a measurement is meant to capture; it can mask or be mistaken for the signal. Often random, noise is not always random, and its meaning depends on the question: radio static can obscure a broadcast, while chance variation among observations can obscure a pattern in data. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compares useful signal strength with noise, so a higher ratio generally means the signal is easier to distinguish. There is no single formula for every field: one statistical definition compares a sample mean with its standard deviation, while signal measurements may compare signal amplitude with noise's standard deviation. Repeated measurements or filtering can sometimes improve SNR.

key_facts.text: Noise does not have to be sound: radio static and random fluctuations in measurements are examples.
Noise is often random, but it can also be nonrandom; whether something counts as noise depends on what information you are trying to detect.
A higher signal-to-noise ratio generally means the useful signal is stronger relative to interference and easier to distinguish.
There are different SNR definitions. NIST describes one statistical version as sample mean divided by sample standard deviation, for suitable ratio-scale data.
When the underlying signal repeats consistently and the noise is random, averaging repeated measurements can make the signal clearer.
